newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy Ross takes crisis mission to Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross takes crisis mission to Israel.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy, fresh from meeting Yasser Arafat in Morocco on Thursday, headed his Middle East crisis mission to Israel for talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The envoy, Dennis Ross, met the Palestinian president for almost two hours in the Moroccan capital Rabat at the start of a lightning bid to get Israelis and Palestinians to stop fighting and start talking. Ross described the talks as "very thorough".
He then left for Israel where he would meet Netanyahu late in the day and again on Friday along with Israel's foreign and defence ministers.
Israel-Palestinian ties plunged into turmoil last week when Netanyahu's government broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Clashes spurred by the construction entered an eighth day on Thursday. About 200 Palestinians hurled stones at Israeli troops who responded by firing rubber bullets and tear gas near Ramallah.
Ross told Reuters in Rabat he would return to Washington by the weekend to report to Clinton so the "president can decide what the next proper move should be".

Israeli political analysts said Ross faced as tall an order as he did last year when -- after a wave of violence claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis -- he brokered Israel's handover of most of Hebron to self-rule.

They said Ross could devise a formula by which Arafat would recommit to fight violence and Netanyahu would promise not to take any more unilateral steps such as last week's groundbreaking on the Jewish settlement.
Israel again urged Ross to press Arafat to crack down on Moslem militant groups. Last Friday a Palestinian suicide bomber blew himself up at a Tel Aviv cafe, killing three Israeli women.
Hamas group, which claimed responsibility for the bombing, has said Israel must expect more bombings.

Russia, co-sponsor with Washington of the Middle East peace process, took Israel to task over the West Bank clashes, citing the settlement construction as the cause of the unrest. A Russian foreign ministry spokesman rejected Israeli charges Arafat had effectively given a "green light" for the bombing.
But as Ross bore messages to Arafat and Netanyahu, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called on the Palestinian leader to give a "red light" to stop guerrilla attacks against Israel.
Israeli military officials warned of a potential surge of unrest climaxing on Sunday -- the annual "Land Day" when Israeli Arabs stage protests against government confiscation of lands.
Israel's Defence Ministry said the army would station tanks at the outskirts of Palestinian-ruled cities if needed to deter stone-throwers from charging soldiers at Israeli outposts.
Arafat was in Rabat to join 15 foreign ministers from Islamic countries at a meeting of the Jerusalem Committee called by Morocco's King Hassan over Israel's new settlement project.
Hamas appealed on Thursday to the Moslem leaders meeting in Morocco to ban normalisation of ties with Israel in an effort to press the Jewish state to halt the "Judaisation" of Jerusalem.

Palestinians urged Ross to lean on Israel to halt work on the East Jerusalem hilltop settlement which the Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and the Israelis call Har Homa. Palestinians regard East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War, as the future capital of an independent Palestinian state.
At the settlement site itself, Israeli authorities said they had found three caves but insisted building would go ahead even if it turned out they contained ancient Jewish graves.
Ultra-orthodox Jews have in the past protested at sites accusing workmen of desecrating ancient Jewish graves and delaying construction.

At the United Nations, the Arab group of states planned to request an emergency special session of the General Assembly on Israel's building of homes for Jews in East Jerusalem following two U.S. vetoes in the Security Council.
